    01 · Know the exam

    Pattern before preparation

    Use the paper structure to decide what deserves time. Prelims demands breadth and accuracy; Mains rewards recall, judgement and written expression.

    150 questions

    General Studies in objective format; 150 marks and 2 hours are indicated in current cycle summaries.

    Negative marking

    Current summaries report one-third deduction. Follow the exact OMR instructions, including the unattempted option, in your notice.

    Screening only

    Prelims scores select candidates for Mains; they do not usually enter the final merit total.

    General Hindi

    Qualifying paper. Do not neglect grammar, précis, comprehension and expression; a failure here can stop evaluation of merit papers.

    Merit papers

    General Studies I, General Studies II and Essay form the descriptive core in current summaries. Optional treatment has varied by cycle.

    Write to score

    Answers need structure, Bihar examples, relevant data and a balanced conclusion—not a dump of memorised notes.

    Personality

    Clarity, honesty, composure, administrative judgement and awareness matter more than theatrical confidence.

    Bihar lens

    Prepare your district, graduation subject, work profile, state challenges, development priorities and recent public issues.

    DAF command

    Every word you submit can become a question. Build short, evidence-based talking points around it.

    Non-negotiable: read the official advertisement, corrigenda and admit-card instructions for your own cycle. Eligibility, reservations, qualifying papers and marking can differ.
    02 · Complete syllabus map

    Turn the syllabus into work units

    Open each block. Every bullet is a revision bucket: learn it, attach Bihar examples, solve PYQs, then compress it into one-page notes.

    History of India & Bihar
    • Ancient: Indus, Vedic age, Buddhism/Jainism, Magadha, Maurya and Gupta periods
    • Medieval: Sultanate, Mughals, Bhakti–Sufi traditions, regional developments
    • Modern: Company rule, 1857, reform movements, nationalism and independence
    • Bihar: ancient centres, Champaran, Kunwar Singh, Rajendra Prasad, social movements and culture
    Geography of India & Bihar
    • Physical geography, climate, monsoon, soils, agriculture and resources
    • Population, settlements, industry, transport and disaster geography
    • Bihar physiography, river systems, floods, irrigation, crops, minerals and regional variation
    • Map practice: rivers, districts, protected areas, heritage and economic locations
    Polity & governance
    • Constitution, rights, duties, DPSP, Parliament, judiciary and federalism
    • State executive and legislature, local government, elections and constitutional bodies
    • Panchayati Raj, community development, planning and Bihar administration
    • Major governance debates, welfare delivery and accountability tools
    Economy: India & Bihar
    • National income, inflation, fiscal and monetary policy, banking and external sector
    • Agriculture, industry, infrastructure, poverty, employment and development
    • Post-independence changes in Bihar; state finances, migration and regional imbalance
    • Read the latest Union and Bihar Budget/Economic Survey for facts and examples
    General science & technology
    • Everyday physics, chemistry and biology at school-foundation level
    • Health, nutrition, disease, biotechnology and public-health applications
    • Space, digital technology, energy, environment and emerging technology
    • Prefer concepts and applications over specialist detail
    Current affairs & mental ability
    • National, international and Bihar events linked to syllabus themes
    • Government schemes, reports, indices, laws, environment and science
    • Percentages, ratios, averages, basic arithmetic, logic and data interpretation
    • Practice in timed mixed sets; keep an error log by concept
    100qualifying

    General Hindi

    Grammar, vocabulary, comprehension, précis and composition. Build a weekly practice slot from day one.

    300merit

    300merit

    03 · Your scoring edge

    Build a Bihar notebook, not a trivia dump

    For every national topic, ask: what does this mean for Bihar? That link turns generic preparation into BPSC preparation.

    History & cultureMagadha, Nalanda–Vikramshila, Buddhism/Jainism, Pala art, Sufi centres, 1857, Champaran, regional languages, fairs and heritage.
    Rivers & disastersGanga basin, Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Son, flood–drought pattern, embankments, wetlands and disaster governance.
    Economy & livelihoodsAgriculture, landholding, migration, MSMEs, food processing, infrastructure, urbanisation, state finances and human development.
    Polity & administrationPanchayati Raj, municipalities, social justice, service delivery, law and order, digital governance and Centre–state relations.
    SocietyPopulation, education, health, nutrition, women, youth, caste and community—always with balanced, constitutional language.
    EnvironmentValmiki landscape, Gangetic dolphin, wetlands, air pollution, groundwater, climate resilience and sustainable agriculture.

    The six-page Bihar file

    1. History timeline ancient → present2. District map rivers + regions3. Economy sheet survey + budget4. Scheme tracker problem → intervention5. Issue briefs cause → solution6. Data bank source + year
    04 · Starter study kit

    Learn, test, then write

    Use these compact notes as a first revision sheet—not as a substitute for the full sources and previous papers linked below.

    Bihar high-yield revision

    Magadha and the imperial core

    South Bihar’s location near iron resources, fertile plains and river routes supported Magadha’s expansion. Rajagriha and later Pataliputra became political centres; the Mauryas projected administration, trade and Buddhism far beyond the region.

    Bihar in the freedom movement

    Kunwar Singh became a major leader of the 1857 uprising in Bihar. Gandhi’s 1917 Champaran Satyagraha investigated indigo cultivators’ grievances and established an early model of mass, evidence-based political action.

    River geography

    The Ganga divides north and south Bihar. Himalayan tributaries such as the Kosi, Gandak and Bagmati carry heavy sediment and create recurring flood risk; southern rivers include the Son and Punpun. Link physical geography to embankments, drainage, livelihoods and disaster management.

    Economy answer frame

    For any Bihar-economy answer, cover structure of output and employment, agriculture productivity, migration, human capital, infrastructure, urbanisation, public finance and regional disparity. End with measurable, district-sensitive interventions.

    Governance answer frame

    Start from constitutional or legal responsibility, identify capacity and last-mile gaps, add local-body and technology roles, protect inclusion and grievance redress, then propose monitoring indicators.

    1. Champaran Satyagraha took place in which year?
    Answer: 1917
    It centred on the grievances of indigo cultivators and marked Gandhi’s first major satyagraha in India.
    2. Which river is often called the “Sorrow of Bihar”?
    Answer: Kosi
    Its sediment load and shifting channels have historically contributed to severe flooding in north Bihar.
    3. The ancient university of Vikramshila is associated with which dynasty?
    Answer: Pala dynasty
    It was a major Buddhist centre of learning in the early medieval period.
    4. Which Article provides for a Finance Commission?
    Answer: Article 280
    The Finance Commission recommends the distribution of certain revenues between the Union and states.
    5. What does fiscal deficit broadly measure?
    Answer: Total expenditure minus total non-borrowing receipts
    It indicates the government’s borrowing requirement for the year.
    6. Why is the Bihar Economic Survey useful in Mains?
    Answer: It supplies current, state-specific evidence
    Use its dated figures, sector trends and district comparisons to support analysis—not as isolated trivia.

    Model Mains skeleton

    Question: “Floods in Bihar are both a geographical and governance challenge.” Discuss.

    1. Intro: locate north Bihar in the Himalayan river system.
    2. Geography: monsoon concentration, sediment, low gradient and changing channels.
    3. Governance: land use, drainage, embankment maintenance, warning systems and coordination.
    4. Impact: crops, health, schooling, migration and infrastructure.
    5. Way forward: basin-level cooperation, floodplain zoning, resilient infrastructure, wetland restoration, local preparedness and transparent relief.

    1. Ancient Indian History

    Harappan town planning — the grid city

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Saptanga — the seven limbs of the state (Kautilya)

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    1.1 Prehistory & the Harappan Civilisation

    Indian history conventionally begins with the Stone Age. The Palaeolithic toolkit appears at sites like Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu) and the Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh) — the latter a UNESCO site with paintings spanning the Upper Palaeolithic to historic times. Mehrgarh (in present-day Pakistan, c. 7000 BCE) shows the earliest farming settlement in the subcontinent and is the direct precursor of the Harappan culture.

    The Harappan/Indus Valley Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE, mature phase) was a Bronze Age, urban, undeciphered-script civilisation spread across present-day Pakistan, western India and Afghanistan — the largest of the three early river-valley civilisations. Its hallmarks: grid-pattern town planning, the Great Bath, standardised weights, and long-distance trade (Mesopotamian texts call it Meluhha). Exam trap: the script remains undeciphered, so unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia we have no readable royal inscriptions — most of what we know comes from archaeology.

    SiteModern locationFamous for
    MohenjodaroSindh, PakistanGreat Bath, dancing-girl bronze
    HarappaPunjab, PakistanGranaries, first discovered (1921, R.D. Banerji at Mohenjodaro; Daya Ram Sahni at Harappa)
    LothalGujaratDockyard — evidence of maritime trade
    DholaviraGujarat (Kutch)Advanced water management; UNESCO World Heritage 2021
    KalibanganRajasthanPloughed field — earliest evidence of plough agriculture
    ChanhudaroSindhBead-making factory (no citadel found here)
    BanawaliHaryanaRadial streets, toy plough
    RakhigarhiHaryanaLargest Harappan site in India

    Decline theories: tectonic/river-course change (Saraswati/Ghaggar drying), floods, Aryan incursion (now largely discounted as sole cause), and climate aridification. BPSC often asks which site is associated with what — the table above is the high-yield core.

    1.2 Vedic Age (c. 1500–600 BCE)

    The Early/Rig Vedic period (1500–1000 BCE) is known from the Rig Veda, the oldest text in the Indo-Aryan corpus, composed in the Sapta-Sindhu (land of seven rivers). Society was tribal-pastoral; the Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) on the Parushni (Ravi) saw Sudas of the Bharatas defeat a confederacy — the region later called Bharatavarsha. Assemblies: Sabha, Samiti, Vidhata, Gana. Women scholars like Gargi and Maitreyi appear; Lopamudra composed Rig Vedic hymns.

    The Later Vedic period (1000–600 BCE) shifted east to the Ganga plain, with settled agriculture, iron (krishna ayas), and the compilation of the Sama Veda (music), Yajur Veda (ritual formulas) and Atharva Veda (magic/medicine), plus the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and the principal Upanishads (the Vedanta — end of the Veda). Exam trap: Satyameva Jayate is from the Mundaka Upanishad.

    1.3 Mahajanapadas & the Rise of Magadha (6th c. BCE)

    Second urbanisation produced 16 Mahajanapadas (listed in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and Jain Bhagavati Sutra). The four great powers: Magadha, Kosala, Vajji (Vrijji/Lichchhavi confederacy — a republic), and Avanti. Magadha's rise rested on five advantages BPSC loves to test: fertile alluvial soil, iron deposits (Rajgir hills), elephants for war, a strategic capital (first Rajagriha, then Pataliputra), and an unorthodox, expansionist monarchy.

    DynastyKey rulersNotes
    Haryanka (544–412 BCE)Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, UdayinBimbisara — first great Magadhan king; Ajatashatru fortified Pataliputra; Udayin founded Pataliputra as capital
    Shishunaga (412–344 BCE)Shishunaga, Kalashoka2nd Buddhist council at Vaishali held under Kalashoka (383 BCE)
    Nanda (344–321 BCE)Mahapadma Nanda, Dhana NandaFirst non-Kshatriya dynasty; vast army and treasury; overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya

    1.4 Buddhism & Jainism

    Both arose as shramana reactions to Vedic ritualism in the 6th century BCE — in Magadha, which is why Bihar is sacred ground for both faiths.

    • Mahavira (599–527 BCE), 24th Tirthankara; born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, attained kevalin at Jrimbhikagrama, attained nirvana at Pavapuri (Pawapuri), Nalanda district, Bihar. Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya (the fifth added by Mahavira). Jain councils: Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE, Sthulabhadra) and Vallabhi (512 CE) — after which the Shvetambara/Digambara split hardened.
    • Gautama Buddha (563–483 BCE): born Lumbini, enlightenment Bodh Gaya (under the Bodhi tree, on the Niranjana riverbank), first sermon Sarnath (Dhammachakkappavattana), mahaparinirvana Kushinagar. Teachings: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Madhyama Marga (middle path), anatman. Exam trap: Buddha is silent on God — he neither affirms nor denies.
    Buddhist CouncilPlacePatron / President
    1st (483 BCE)RajagrihaAjatshatru / Mahakassapa — Sutta and Vinaya compiled
    2nd (383 BCE)VaishaliKalashoka / Sabbakami — first schism
    3rd (250 BCE)PataliputraAshoka / Moggaliputta Tissa — Theravada canon fixed; missions sent abroad
    4th (1st c. CE)Kundalvana, KashmirKanishka / Vasumitra — Mahayana/Hinayana split formalised

    1.5 Mauryan Empire (321–185 BCE)

    Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire with Chanakya/Kautilya/Vishnugupta (author of the Arthashastra). He defeated Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE); Megasthenes' Indica describes Pataliputra. Bindusara (Amitraghata) followed; then Ashoka (268–232 BCE), whose Kalinga war (261 BCE) converted him to Dhamma — a moral code preached through rock and pillar edicts in Prakrit (Brahmi script). The Sarnath Lion Capital is India's national emblem; the Dharmachakra is on the flag. Provincial capitals: Taxila, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri, Tosali. Last Maurya Brihadratha was assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga (185 BCE).

    Exam traps: Kalinga war = 261 BCE; the 3rd Buddhist council at Pataliputra was Ashoka's; the Arthashastra is about statecraft, not economics alone; Indica survives only in fragments quoted by later writers.

    1.6 Post-Mauryan Age & the Guptas

    After the Mauryas: Shungas (Pushyamitra; Bharhut stupa), Kanvas, Satavahanas (Deccan; Gautamiputra Satakarni; Nasik/Karle caves), Indo-Greeks (Menander/Milinda — Milindapanho dialogue with Nagasena), Shakas (Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription — earliest long Sanskrit inscription), Kushanas (Kanishka: started the Shaka era, 78 CE; Gandhara and Mathura art flourished).

    The Gupta Age (c. 320–550 CE) is called the classical/golden age — but BPSC expects specifics, not adjectives:

    • Chandragupta I (320–335): founder of the Gupta era (319–320 CE); married Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi.
    • Samudragupta (335–380): the Allahabad pillar inscription by Harishena records his digvijaya; V.A. Smith called him the "Napoleon of India". Coins show him playing the veena.
    • Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (380–415): Ujjain made second capital; Navratna court — Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta), Varahamihira (Brihat Samhita), Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE — place value, zero, pi approximation, earth's rotation), Dhanvantari, Amarasimha (Amarakosha).
    • Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda Mahavihara (Bihar). Chinese pilgrim Faxian (Fa-Hien) visited during Chandragupta II's reign.
    • Administration: provinces = bhukti, districts = vishaya; land grants (agraharas) to Brahmanas mark the beginnings of feudalism.

    1.7 Harsha & the Early Medieval Transition

    Harshavardhana (606–647 CE) of Thanesar/Kannauj: Banabhatta's Harshacharita and Hiuen Tsang's Si-yu-ki are the key sources. Hiuen Tsang attended the Kannauj assembly and the Prayag (Allahabad) quinquennial alms-giving. Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas on the Narmada — the classic north–south check. His death (647) ends ancient Indian history in most BPSC framing; the Palas then dominate Bihar/Bengal (see Medieval chapter). In the south, the Pallavas (Mahabalipuram shore temple), Chalukyas of Badami, and later the Cholas (Rajaraja I, 985–1014 — Brihadeshwara temple, Thanjavur; Rajendra I founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram after his Ganga expedition) complete the picture.

    Quick revision hooks: 261 BCE Kalinga · 78 CE Shaka era · 319–320 CE Gupta era · Pavapuri = Mahavira's nirvana (Bihar) · Pataliputra = 3rd Buddhist council + Mauryan capital · Nalanda = Kumaragupta I · Dholavira = water management · Kalibangan = ploughed field.

    2.1 The Tripartite Struggle & the Pala Empire (c. 750–1200)

    After Harsha, north India saw the tripartite struggle for Kannauj among the Gurjara-Pratiharas (west), Palas (east) and Rashtrakutas (Deccan). For BPSC, the Palas matter most — they ruled Bihar and Bengal for four centuries, the longest continuous rule over this region in the medieval period.

    • Gopala (c. 750): founder, elected by the people (prakriti) after a century of anarchy (matsyanyaya); built Odantapuri Mahavihara (Bihar Sharif area).
    • Dharmapala (c. 770–810): greatest Pala king; founded Vikramashila Mahavihara (near Bhagalpur, on the Ganga) and revived Nalanda. The Khalimpur copper plate records his reign.
    • Devapala: extended Pala power to Assam and Orissa; Tibetan records mention his patronage of Buddhism.
    • Later Palas declined under Kaivarta revolt (Divya's uprising, c. 11th century); the dynasty ended when Bakhtiyar Khilji sacked Nalanda and Vikramashila (~1193 CE) — the conventional end of ancient/medieval Buddhist learning in Bihar.

    Pala art: the distinctive black-basalt Buddhist sculpture of Bihar/Bengal and the Pala school of miniature painting (manuscript illustration — among the earliest Indian miniatures). Exam trap: Vikramashila = Dharmapala; Odantapuri = Gopala; Nalanda = Kumaragupta I (Gupta, not Pala — Palas only patronised it).

    Contemporaries to know briefly: Mihir Bhoja (Pratihara), Amoghavarsha (Rashtrakuta, Jain patron, Kavirajamarga), and in the south the Cholas — Rajaraja I (985–1014) built the Brihadeshwara temple, Thanjavur, and maintained a powerful navy; Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda after his expedition to the Ganga.

    2.2 Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)

    Founded after Muizzuddin Muhammad Ghori's victories at Tarain — 1191 (Prithviraj III Chauhan won the first), 1192 (Ghori won the second) — the decisive battle that opened north India to Turkic rule. Five dynasties:

    DynastyKey rulers & facts
    Slave/Mamluk (1206–90)Qutb-ud-din Aibak (founder; began Qutub Minar; built Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque); Iltutmish (real founder — iqta system, silver tanka and copper jital, completed Qutub Minar); Razia Sultana (1236–40 — first and only woman Sultan of Delhi); Balban (zaminbos prostration, sijda, diwan-i-arz military department)
    Khalji (1290–1320)Alauddin Khalji — market-price control (diwan-i-riyasat), dagh (horse branding) and chehra; repelled Mongols; Malik Kafur's Deccan campaigns
    Tughlaq (1320–1414)Ghiyasuddin; Muhammad bin Tughlaq — token currency (failed), capital transfer to Daulatabad (failed), raised land tax in Doab; Firoz Shah Tughlaq — canals, diwan-i-khairat (charity), founded Jaunpur and Hissar
    Sayyid (1414–51)Khizr Khan — weakest dynasty, Timur's aftermath
    Lodi (1451–1526)Bahlol; Sikandar (founded Agra, 1504); Ibrahim Lodi — defeated by Babur at Panipat, 1526

    Exam traps: Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak but completed by Iltutmish; Razia ruled 1236–40; token currency and Daulatabad are both Muhammad bin Tughlaq's failures; the Sultanate's official language of administration was Persian.

    2.3 Vijayanagara (1336–1646)

    Founded by Harihara and Bukka (Sangama dynasty) on the Tungabhadra, with the blessings of Vidyaranya. Greatest ruler: Krishnadevaraya (1509–29) — author of Amuktamalyada (Telugu), patron of the Ashtadiggajas (eight Telugu poets); foreign travellers Domingo Paes and Nicolo Conti describe Hampi's splendour. The empire fell after the Battle of Talikota (1565) against the Deccan Sultanates. Architecture: Virupaksha and Vittala temples at Hampi (UNESCO).

    2.4 Bhakti & Sufi Movements

    The Bhakti movement (6th–17th c.) democratised devotion — vernacular languages, rejection of caste exclusivity, personal god:

    • South (Alvars & Nayanars, 6th–9th c.): Tamil devotional roots; Shankara (Advaita), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhva (Dvaita).
    • North: Kabir (nirguna, weaver of Varanasi; dohas compiled in Bijak), Guru Nanak (1469–1539; Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan), Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (Gaudiya Vaishnavism, Bengal), Mirabai (Krishna bhakti, Rajasthan), Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas, Awadhi; contemporary of Akbar), Surdas (Sursagar).
    • Bihar link: the Sufi saint Makhdoom Yahya Maneri of Bihar Sharif (Suhrawardi/Firdausi order) and the Khanqah-e-Muazzam tradition.

    Sufi silsilas: Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti, Ajmer; Nizamuddin Auliya, Delhi; sama/qawwali), Suhrawardi (Bahauddin Zakariya, Multan — accepted state patronage, unlike the Chishtis), Qadiri, Naqshbandi (Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi — Mujaddid, opposed Akbar's eclecticism). Exam trap: Chishtis stayed aloof from the court; Suhrawardis did not.

    2.5 The Mughals (1526–1857)

    • Babur (1526–30): Panipat 1526 (gunpowder + tulughma tactics), Khanwa 1527 (Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (Medini Rai), Ghaghra 1529 (Afghans). Memoirs: Tuzuk-i-Baburi/Baburnama (Chagatai Turkish).
    • Humayun (1530–40, 1555–56): defeated by Sher Shah Suri at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj/Bilgram (1540); died falling from his library stairs.
    • Sher Shah Suri (1540–45) — Bihar's own emperor, born in Sasaram: introduced the silver rupiya (ancestor of the rupee), built the Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-e-Azam, from Sonargaon to Peshawar), reformed land revenue (zabt, measured fields, patta and qabuliyat), built his mausoleum at Sasaram and fortified Rohtasgarh. Died at Kalinjar (1545).
    • Akbar (1556–1605): regent Bairam Khan; 2nd Battle of Panipat 1556 (Hemu defeated); abolished jizya (1564) and pilgrim tax; Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri; Din-i-Ilahi (1582) — only Birbal fully embraced it; mansabdari system; zabt revenue under Todar Mal; Akbarnama/Ain-i-Akbari by Abul Fazl.
    • Jahangir (1605–27): chain of justice; Nur Jahan's influence; Captain Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe (1615) at court.
    • Shah Jahan (1628–58): Taj Mahal (1632–53), Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Peacock Throne; deposed by Aurangzeb.
    • Aurangzeb (1658–1707): reimposed jizya (1679), longest Deccan wars, executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675); empire at its largest — and most overstretched.

    Decline: weak successors, Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi (1739) and the Battle of Plassey (1757) finished Mughal power; Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last emperor, exiled after 1857.

    2.6 The Marathas

    Shivaji (1630–80): coronation at Raigad, 1674 (Chhatrapati); administration — ashtapradhan council, forts (Purandar, Sinhagad), guerrilla warfare (ganimi kava); revenue — chauth (1/4) and sardeshmukhi (1/10). Peshwas: Balaji Vishwanath (founder of Peshwa dominance), Baji Rao I (greatest expansionist), Balaji Baji Rao — defeat at 3rd Battle of Panipat, 1761 (Ahmad Shah Abdali). Anglo-Maratha wars ended with the annexation of 1818.

    Quick revision hooks: Tarain 1192 · Qutub Minar: begun Aibak, finished Iltutmish · Razia 1236–40 · Talikota 1565 · Din-i-Ilahi 1582 · Chausa 1539 / Bilgram 1540 (Sher Shah beats Humayun) · Sasaram = Sher Shah's tomb · Vikramashila = Dharmapala.

    3. Modern History & the Freedom Movement

    Revolutionary nationalism — events spine

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    3.1 The British Arrive (1600–1765)

    The English East India Company was chartered on 31 December 1600. Early footholds: Surat factory (1613), Madras (Fort St. George, 1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta (Fort William, 1700). The Carnatic Wars eliminated French rivalry (Battle of Wandiwash, 1760). Then the decisive sequence in Bengal:

    EventYearSignificance
    Battle of Plassey1757Clive defeated Siraj-ud-daulah (betrayed by Mir Jafar); British became kingmakers in Bengal
    Battle of Buxar22 Oct 1764Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-daulah (Awadh) and Shah Alam II — fought on Bihar's soil; real beginning of British territorial empire
    Treaty of Allahabad1765Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted to the Company — dual government begins

    Exam trap: Plassey made the British influential; Buxar made them sovereign. BPSC asks this distinction directly, and Buxar's Bihar location is a favourite fact.

    3.2 Land Revenue & Early Resistance

    • Permanent Settlement (1793), Cornwallis — Bengal, Bihar, Orissa: zamindars made hereditary owners; fixed revenue; led to absentee landlordism and peasant misery in Bihar.
    • Ryotwari (Munro, Madras/Bombay) and Mahalwari (Mackenzie, North-West) systems.
    • Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley) and Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie) — annexations of Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Awadh (1856).

    Pre-1857 revolts with Bihar links: the Santhal Rebellion (1855–56) — Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu rose in the Rajmahal hills against zamindars and moneylenders (the Santhal Pargana now lies in Jharkhand, but the revolt's administrative response created the region's first tribal protections); the Wahabi movement had centres in Patna and Saran under Syed Ahmad Barelvi's followers.

    3.3 The Revolt of 1857

    Causes: political (Doctrine of Lapse), economic (drain of wealth — Dadabhai Naoroji's thesis), social-religious (the greased cartridges were the spark, not the cause). Timeline: Mangal Pandey, Barrackpore, 29 March 1857; Meerut, 10 May 1857; Delhi seized, Bahadur Shah Zafar declared emperor.

    CentreLeader
    DelhiBahadur Shah Zafar (nominal), Bakht Khan (military)
    LucknowBegum Hazrat Mahal
    KanpurNana Sahib, Tantia Tope
    JhansiRani Lakshmibai
    Bihar (Jagdispur/Arrah)Kunwar Singh (Veer Kunwar Singh) — aged ~80, led the siege of Arrah (1857), defeated Captain Dunbar, died 26 April 1858
    BareillyKhan Bahadur Khan

    Result: the Government of India Act 1858 — Crown rule, Governor-General became Viceroy (Canning), Queen Victoria's Proclamation. Exam trap: the revolt is called the First War of Independence by V.D. Savarkar (The Indian War of Independence, 1857).

    3.4 The Indian National Congress & Early Nationalism

    • INC founded December 1885, Bombay — by A.O. Hume; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; 72 delegates.
    • Moderates (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta): petitions, drain theory.
    • Partition of Bengal (1905, Curzon) → Swadeshi & Boycott movement; annulled 1911 (Delhi Durbar; capital shifted to Delhi).
    • Surat Split (1907): Moderates vs Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal — Lal-Bal-Pal).
    • Morley-Minto Reforms 1909: separate electorates for Muslims — "divide and rule" seed.
    • Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress–Muslim League agreement; Home Rule Movement (Tilak, Annie Besant).

    3.5 The Gandhian Era — with Bihar at the Centre

    • Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, at the invitation of Rajkumar Shukla, against the tinkathia system (forced indigo cultivation on 3/20th of land) in Champaran, Bihar. This is the single most-asked Bihar fact in BPSC history papers.
    • Kheda (1918) and Ahmedabad mill strike (1918) followed.
    • Rowlatt Act (1919) → Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919 (General Dyer, Amritsar).
    • Non-Cooperation (1920–22): launched after Khilafat + Punjab wrongs; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (5 Feb 1922).
    • Civil Disobedience (1930): Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930); Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); 2nd Round Table Conference (Gandhi attended); Poona Pact (1932) with Ambedkar after the Communal Award.
    • Government of India Act 1935: provincial autonomy; 1937 elections — Congress ministries; in Bihar Sri Krishna Singh became Premier.

    3.6 Quit India & the Road to Independence

    • Quit India Movement (8 August 1942) — "Do or Die" (Karenge ya Marenge). Bihar's finest hour: on 11 August 1942, seven students were shot dead at the Patna Secretariat while hoisting the flag — the Shaheed Smarak (Martyrs' Memorial) in Patna commemorates them (Saat Shaheed).
    • Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) — Bihar's own: escaped from Hazaribagh Central Jail (1942), organised underground resistance; decades later he would lead the Sampoorna Kranti (1974).
    • INA & Subhas Chandra Bose: "Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom" (Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga); Delhi Chalo; INA trials at Red Fort (1945–46).
    • Cabinet Mission (1946), Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947), Indian Independence Act — independence 15 August 1947; first Governor-General Lord Mountbatten, first Indian Governor-General C. Rajagopalachari; first PM Jawaharlal Nehru, first President Dr. Rajendra Prasad (from Bihar).
    • Bihar milestones: Bihar and Orissa province created 1912 (separated from Bengal); Bihar became a separate province in 1936 (Orissa carved out); Sri Krishna Singh first Chief Minister (1946); Jharkhand carved out 15 November 2000.

    Quick revision hooks: Plassey 1757 · Buxar 1764 · Permanent Settlement 1793 · Mangal Pandey 29 Mar 1857 · INC 1885 Bombay · Partition of Bengal 1905 · Champaran 1917 (first satyagraha) · Jallianwala 13 Apr 1919 · Chauri Chaura 1922 · Dandi 1930 · Patna Secretariat 11 Aug 1942 (7 martyrs) · 15 Aug 1947.

    4. Bihar History & Culture

    Bihar Buddhist circuit — four great sites

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    4.1 Ancient Bihar — the Cradle of Empires

    Bihar is not a footnote in Indian history — for a thousand years it was Indian history. Magadha, centred on present-day south Bihar, produced India's first great empires: the Haryankas, Shishunagas, Nandas and Mauryas (Chandragupta, Ashoka — see Chapter 1). Capitals: Rajagriha (Rajgir), then Pataliputra (Patna), one of the ancient world's great cities — Megasthenes described its wooden palisade with 570 towers.

    • Vaishali — capital of the Lichchhavi confederacy, described as one of the world's earliest republics (gana-sangha); Buddha praised its governance; the 2nd Buddhist council met here (383 BCE).
    • Bodh Gaya — Buddha's enlightenment; the Mahabodhi Temple (UNESCO World Heritage) was built substantially in Gupta times.
    • Pavapuri (Pawapuri), Nalanda district — Mahavira's nirvana; the Jalmandir temple stands in a lotus tank.
    • Nalanda Mahavihara (founded by Kumaragupta I, 5th c.) — the world's first residential university: 10,000 students, 2,000 teachers, a nine-storey library (Ratnasagara); Hiuen Tsang studied here. Destroyed c. 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khilji. UNESCO World Heritage (2016).
    • Vikramashila (Dharmapala, Pala king — near Bhagalpur) and Odantapuri (Gopala — near Bihar Sharif) completed the "five great mahaviharas" of the Pala age.
    • Chirand (Saran district) — a Neolithic-Chalcolithic site on the Saryu-Ganga confluence, showing continuous settlement from c. 2500 BCE.

    Mauryan art in Bihar: the polished Didarganj Yakshi (now in Patna Museum) and the Ashokan pillars at Lauriya Nandangarh, Lauriya Areraj and Rampurva (West/East Champaran) — the lion and bull capitals are the finest surviving Mauryan sculpture.

    4.2 Medieval & Early Modern Bihar

    • Sher Shah Suri (1540–45) — born in Sasaram (Rohtas district); his Indo-Islamic mausoleum at Sasaram stands mid-lake, and he fortified Rohtasgarh Fort. The Grand Trunk Road and the rupiya are his gifts to India.
    • Sufi Bihar: Makhdoom Yahya Maneri (d. 1380) of Bihar Sharif — the Firdausi saint whose Maktubat (letters) are a classic of Indo-Persian literature; the Khanqah-e-Muazzam at Bihar Sharif.
    • Battle of Buxar (1764) on Bihar's soil transferred the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company. The Patna region became a great opium and saltpetre entrepôt; Golghar (1786, Captain John Garstin) was built as a famine granary.
    • 1857: Veer Kunwar Singh of Jagdispur (Bhojpur); the siege of Arrah. 1912: Bihar and Orissa province carved from Bengal with Patna as capital. 1917: Champaran Satyagraha. 1936: separate Bihar province. 1942: Saat Shaheed of Patna Secretariat; JP's Hazaribagh escape.
    • Post-independence: Dr. Rajendra Prasad, India's first President, was from Ziradei (Siwan); Jayaprakash Narayan (Sitab Diara, Saran) led the Sampoorna Kranti movement (1974) from Patna; Karpoori Thakur pioneered backward-class reservations as CM. 15 November 2000: Jharkhand bifurcated from Bihar.

    4.3 Languages of Bihar

    LanguageRegionNotes
    MaithiliMithila (Darbhanga, Madhubani, Saharsa…)Included in the 8th Schedule by the 92nd Amendment, 2003; classical literature — Vidyapati (14th–15th c., Padavali); own script Tirhuta/Mithilakshar
    BhojpuriWest Bihar (Bhojpur, Saran, Champaran)Named after Raja Bhoj's Ujjain/Bhojpur; Bhikhari Thakur — "Shakespeare of Bhojpuri", creator of Bideshiya folk theatre
    MagahiSouth Bihar (Gaya, Patna, Nalanda)Direct descendant of Magadhi Prakrit — the language of the Buddha's sermons and Ashokan edicts

    Exam trap: Maithili is the only Bihar language in the 8th Schedule; Bhojpuri is not (a perennial demand). Hindi and Urdu are the state's official languages.

    4.4 Art, Craft & GI Tags

    • Madhubani/Mithila painting — wall-and-paper art of the Mithila region; styles bharni (filled) and kachni (line); masters Sita Devi, Ganga Devi, Mahasundari Devi; GI tagged.
    • GI tags of Bihar (memorise as a set): Shahi Litchi (Muzaffarpur), Mithila Makhana, Bhagalpuri Silk, Katarni Rice (Bhagalpur), Magahi Paan, Sikki Grass products, Jardalu Mango (Bhagalpur), Marcha Rice (West Champaran), Sikki craft. BPSC increasingly asks "which district" for each GI product.
    • Sujini embroidery (Bhusra, Muzaffarpur), lac bangles, stone craft of Gaya (Vishnupad), Manjusha art (Bhagalpur — snake-goddess Bishahari lore).

    4.5 Festivals, Fairs & Performing Arts

    • Chhath Puja — Bihar's signature festival: four days ending on Kartik Shukla Shashthi, dedicated to Surya and Chhathi Maiya, with arghya offered at riverbanks/ghats. Also observed as Chaiti Chhath in Chaitra.
    • Sama-Chakeva (Mithila, Kartik — celebrates sibling love), Teej, Jitiya (mothers' fast for children), Sohrai, Karma.
    • Sonepur (Harihar Kshetra) Mela — held at the Ganga-Gandak confluence on Kartik Purnima; Asia's largest cattle fair; anchored by the Hariharnath temple.
    • Pitrapaksha Mela, Gaya — pind-daan at Vishnupad; Shravani Mela, Deoghar (now Jharkhand, but historically the Bihar pilgrim circuit).
    • Folk forms: Jat-Jatin (Mithila, monsoon), Jhijhiya (goddess Durga, Dussehra), Bideshiya dance-drama (Bhikhari Thakur), Domkach (wedding songs); instruments dholak, mandar, bansuri.
    • Cuisine: litti-chokha, sattu preparations, thekua (Chhath prasad), khaja of Silao, tilkut of Gaya.

    Quick revision hooks: Nalanda = Kumaragupta I · Vikramashila = Dharmapala · Pavapuri = Mahavira nirvana · Vaishali = Lichchhavi republic · Sasaram = Sher Shah's tomb · Maithili = 92nd Amendment 2003 · Shahi Litchi = Muzaffarpur · 7 martyrs = Patna Secretariat 11 Aug 1942 · Jharkhand carved out 15 Nov 2000.

    4.x The Freedom Movement in Bihar — an expanded account

    Bihar's contribution to the freedom struggle went far beyond Champaran. In 1857, the revolt reached Bihar through the sepoys of the Danapur cantonment, who mutinied on 25 July 1857 and marched to Arrah to join Kunwar Singh of Jagdispur. At about 80 years old, Kunwar Singh recaptured Arrah, defeated Captain Dunbar's relief force, and carried the rebellion up the Gangetic valley to Lucknow and Azamgarh before dying of his wounds in 1858. His brother Amar Singh continued the guerrilla resistance in the Shahabad hills.

    The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — Gandhi's first satyagraha in India — was triggered by the tinkathia system, under which European indigo planters forced peasants to cultivate indigo on 3/20th of their holdings at fixed, ruinous prices. Persuaded by the peasant leader Raj Kumar Shukla, Gandhi investigated, defied a magisterial order to leave Champaran, and forced the government to appoint the Champaran Agrarian Committee; the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 abolished tinkathia. The team Gandhi assembled — Rajendra Prasad, J.B. Kripalani, Mazharul Haque, Mahadev Desai — became the nucleus of Bihar's Congress leadership.

    In the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), Bihar responded strongly: the Bihar Vidyapeeth was founded at Patna (1921) as a nationalist university under Mazharul Haque's patronage, and Rajendra Prasad abandoned a lucrative law practice. During the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930), Bihar manufactured contraband salt and boycotted foreign cloth under Prasad's leadership; the province's peasants, already organised by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati's Kisan Sabha (founded 1929 in Bihar; All India Kisan Sabha at Lucknow, 1936), fused the agrarian and national struggles.

    The Quit India Movement (1942) saw Bihar at its most militant. On 11 August 1942, police fired on students attempting to hoist the national flag at the Patna Secretariat, killing seven — Umakant Prasad Sinha (aged 14), Ramanand Singh, Satish Prasad Jha, Jagatpati Kumar, Devipada Choudhary, Rajendra Singh and Ramgovind Singh — honoured by the Shaheed Smarak. Jayaprakash Narayan's escape from Hazaribagh Central Jail on 9 November 1942 electrified the underground; his Azad Dasta organised guerrilla resistance in Nepal's Terai and Bihar's border districts. Saran, Champaran and Bhagalpur districts saw prolonged paralysis of British administration.

    4.y Bihar's statehood journey — 1912, 1936, 2000 and beyond

    Modern Bihar was born on 22 March 1912, when Bihar and Orissa were separated from the Bengal Presidency — the date celebrated as Bihar Diwas. The province's boundaries were redrawn in 1936, when Orissa became a separate province under the Government of India Act, 1935. After independence, Bihar's first ministry under Sri Krishna Sinha ("Bihar Kesari") with deputy Anugrah Narayan Sinha (1946–1961) laid the foundations of the modern state — from the Barauni refinery to land-reform legislation.

    The most recent redrawing came on 15 November 2000, when the mineral-rich southern districts were carved out as Jharkhand, leaving Bihar with 38 districts and a predominantly agrarian economy. Culturally, Maithili won constitutional recognition through the 92nd Amendment (2003), entering the Eighth Schedule alongside Bodo, Dogri and Santhali.

    Politically, the state turned a historic page in 2025–26: the November 2025 Assembly elections gave the NDA about 202 of 243 seats, and on 15 April 2026 Samrat Choudhary became the first BJP leader to serve as Chief Minister of Bihar, succeeding Nitish Kumar — a transition every BPSC polity question-set will now probe. For revision, anchor the sequence: 1912 (birth) · 1936 (Orissa out) · 2000 (Jharkhand out) · 2026 (first BJP CM).

    5.1 The Earth — Origin & Interior

    The dominant theory of the universe's origin is the Big Bang; the solar system's formation is explained by the Nebular hypothesis (Kant–Laplace). The Earth is an oblate spheroid (geoid) — slightly flattened at the poles; evidence of rotation: the Foucault pendulum and Coriolis deflection.

    Interior structure (from seismic-wave evidence):

    LayerDepth (approx.)Key facts
    Crust5–70 kmSIAL (continental, granite) and SIMA (oceanic, basalt); separated from mantle by the Mohorovičić discontinuity
    Mantle~2,900 kmAsthenosphere (partially molten, source of magma); separated from core by the Gutenberg discontinuity
    Core2,900–6,371 kmOuter core liquid (source of the magnetic field); inner core solid (immense pressure); mainly nickel-iron (NIFE)

    Exam trap: S-waves cannot pass through liquids — the shadow zone this creates is the proof that the outer core is liquid. P-waves travel through solids and liquids but refract at boundaries.

    5.2 Rocks & Landforms

    TypeFormationExamples
    IgneousCooling of magma/lavaGranite (intrusive), basalt (extrusive — Deccan Traps)
    SedimentaryDeposition & lithificationSandstone, limestone, shale; contain fossils
    MetamorphicHeat/pressure alterationMarble (from limestone), slate (from shale), gneiss (from granite), quartzite (from sandstone)

    Weathering (in-situ breakdown: physical, chemical, biological) vs erosion (transport by agents). Landforms by agent: rivers — V-shaped valleys, meanders, oxbow lakes, deltas; wind — yardangs, mushroom rocks, loess; glaciers — U-shaped valleys, cirques, moraines, fjords; groundwater — stalactites/stalagmites, karst; sea — cliffs, stacks, arches.

    5.3 Plate Tectonics, Earthquakes & Volcanoes

    Plate tectonics (the framework BPSC expects, superseding Wegener's continental drift):

    • Convergent — plates collide: fold mountains (Himalayas: Indo-Australian + Eurasian), deep trenches, volcanic arcs.
    • Divergent — plates separate: mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys (East African Rift).
    • Transform — plates slide past: strike-slip faults (San Andreas).

    Earthquakes: focus/hypocentre (origin) vs epicentre (surface point above); measured on the Richter scale (magnitude) and Mercalli scale (intensity). India: most of the Himalayan belt and Kutch are in high-risk seismic zones IV–V (Bihar falls largely in zone IV — the 1934 Bihar–Nepal earthquake, magnitude ~8.0, is the grim reference).

    Volcanoes: active (Etna, Stromboli — "Lighthouse of the Mediterranean"), dormant, extinct. Types: shield (Mauna Loa, Hawaii — gentle basaltic), composite/stratovolcano (Fujiyama — explosive), cinder cone. Exam trap: India's only active volcano is Barren Island (Andaman & Nicobar); Narcondam is dormant. The Pacific Ring of Fire hosts most of the world's active volcanoes. Tsunamis are most often triggered by undersea earthquakes (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami — Sumatra epicentre).

    5.4 Atmosphere — Structure & Pressure Systems

    LayerHeight (approx.)Notes
    Troposphere0–18 km (equator)All weather happens here; temperature falls with height (normal lapse rate); topped by the tropopause
    Stratosphere18–50 kmOzone layer — absorbs UV; jets fly here
    Mesosphere50–80 kmColdest layer; meteors burn up here
    Thermosphere/Ionosphere80–700 kmAuroras; radio-wave reflection
    Exosphere700 km+Thins into space

    Pressure belts (idealised): equatorial low (doldrums), subtropical highs (~30°), subpolar lows (~60°), polar highs. Planetary winds blow from high to low, deflected by Coriolis (right in the northern hemisphere): trade winds (easterlies, towards equator), westerlies (mid-latitudes), polar easterlies. Local winds to memorise: Loo (hot, north India summer), Chinook (warm, Rockies — "snow eater"), Mistral (cold, France/Spain), Sirocco (hot, Sahara→Mediterranean), Harmattan (dry, West Africa — "doctor wind"). Jet streams in the upper troposphere steer western disturbances that bring winter rain to north India — a direct BPSC link.

    Cyclones: tropical cyclones need warm seas (>27 °C), Coriolis force (absent at the equator — no cyclones within ~5° of the equator), and low wind shear. Regional names: hurricane (Atlantic), typhoon (Pacific), willy-willy (Australia); Indian Ocean cyclones are named from a regional list maintained with IMD participation. Anticyclones bring settled, clear weather. Temperate cyclones form along the polar front.

    5.5 Oceanography & the Water Cycle

    Ocean relief: continental shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain; trenches are the deepest points (Mariana Trench, ~11,000 m). Salinity averages 35‰; highest in enclosed seas (Dead Sea ~240‰, Great Salt Lake). Currents:

    Warm currentsCold currents
    Gulf Stream (Atlantic), Kuroshio (Pacific), Brazil, Agulhas (Indian Ocean)Labrador (Atlantic), Humboldt/Peru (Pacific), Benguela (Atlantic), West Australian, Somali (Indian Ocean — cold in summer, drives upwelling)

    Fishing grounds concentrate where warm and cold currents meet (Grand Banks — Gulf Stream + Labrador; Dogger Bank — North Sea). Tides: caused by the moon's (mainly) and sun's gravity; spring tides (sun–moon–earth aligned, new/full moon) vs neap tides (right angles). Coral reefs need warm (>20 °C), shallow, clear, sunlit water — Lakshadweep (atolls) and the Gulf of Mannar in India; Darwin's subsidence theory explains atoll formation.

    Quick revision hooks: Moho = crust–mantle · Gutenberg = mantle–core · Barren Island = only active Indian volcano · Ozone = stratosphere · 1934 = Bihar–Nepal quake (zone IV) · Mariana Trench deepest · No cyclones near equator · Loo = north Indian summer wind.

    Soils of India — eight types at a glance

    6.1 Physiographic Divisions of India

    • The Himalayas — three parallel ranges: Himadri (Greater Himalayas; peaks: Mt. Everest 8,848 m in Nepal, K2/Godwin-Austen 8,611 m in PoK, Kanchenjunga 8,586 m — highest wholly in India), Himachal (Lesser Himalayas; hill stations — Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling; duns like Dehradun between ranges), Shiwalik (outer foothills). Key passes: Banihal (J&K), Zoji La (Srinagar–Leh), Shipki La (Himachal), Nathu La (Sikkim), Bomdi La (Arunachal). The Pir Panjal is the largest Lesser-Himalayan range.
    • The Northern Plains — bhabar (porous foothill gravels), terai (marshy, re-emerging streams), bhangar (old alluvium), khadar (new, flood-renewed alluvium). Bihar sits squarely in the middle Ganga plain.
    • The Peninsular Plateau — oldest landmass (Gondwana); divided by the Narmada into the Central Highlands (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur) and the Deccan Plateau; the Western Ghats (continuous, higher — Anaimudi 2,695 m) vs the Eastern Ghats (discontinuous).
    • Coastal plains & islands — western coast: Konkan, Kannad, Malabar (narrow, estuaries); eastern: Coromandel, Northern Circars (broad, deltas). Islands: Andaman & Nicobar (volcanic — Barren Island; Saddle Peak highest) and Lakshadweep (coral atolls).

    6.2 Rivers — the Ganga System First (Bihar's Lifeline)

    The Ganga (2,525 km) rises at Gaumukh (Gangotri glacier, Uttarakhand), enters the plains at Haridwar, and meets the Bay of Bengal via the Hooghly (India) and Padma/Meghna (Bangladesh). It is India's longest river and was declared the National River (2008). In Bihar it flows west to east, dividing the state into the north and south plains — every major Bihar tributary joins it.

    RiverOriginJoins GangaNotes
    SonAmarkantak (M.P.)Near Patna (from the south)Largest south-bank tributary; wide sandy bed; Son canal system irrigates south Bihar
    GandakNepal Himalaya (Narayani)Hajipur (from the north)Carries heavy silt; Valmiki Nagar/Gandak project
    KosiSaptakoshi, Nepal/TibetKursela, Katihar (from the north)"Sorrow of Bihar" — shifts course, devastating floods; Kosi project
    GhagharaTibet (Mapchachungo)Chhapra/Revelganj (from the north)Forms part of the Bihar–U.P. boundary
    BagmatiNepalNorth Bihar plainsFlood-prone; originates near Kathmandu
    PunpunChotanagpur plateauFatuha, near Patna (from the south)Sacred for pind-daan; joins near the state capital
    Falgu (Niranjana)Chotanagpur— (flows past Gaya, goes underground)Buddha's enlightenment was on its bank at Bodh Gaya

    Exam traps: the Son is the only major tributary joining from the south near Patna; the Kosi's "sorrow" epithet is a verbatim favourite; the Falgu flows underground at Gaya.

    Other Indian rivers (high-yield set): Yamuna (largest Ganga tributary; originates Yamunotri); Brahmaputra (Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet → Siang/Dihang in Arunachal → Assam; Majuli — world's largest river island); peninsular rivers — Godavari (1,465 km, longest peninsular; "Dakshin Ganga"), Krishna, Kaveri (disputed waters — Karnataka/Tamil Nadu), Mahanadi (Hirakud dam), Narmada (longest west-flowing; rift valley; Sardar Sarovar), Tapi (west-flowing; Surat at its mouth). Trap: Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea; almost all other peninsular rivers flow east. West-flowing rivers form estuaries, not deltas.

    Lakes: Wular (J&K — largest freshwater lake in India), Chilika (Odisha — largest brackish lagoon), Sambhar (Rajasthan — largest inland salt lake), Vembanad (Kerala), Loktak (Manipur — floating phumdis). Bihar wetlands: Kanwar Lake (Begusarai) — Bihar's only Ramsar site of long standing — and Gogabil (Katihar).

Local soil names BPSC may use: bal sundari (sandy), kewal (clayey).

    RabiOct–Nov (winter)Mar–AprWheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas
    ZaidApr–MayJuneWatermelon, cucumber, fodder, vegetables

    Bihar's agriculture: rice is the principal kharif crop; wheat the principal rabi crop; maize (Khagaria–Saharsa belt is a major maize zone); sugarcane (north-west Bihar); jute (Purnia–Katihar–Kishanganj — the "jute belt"); litchi (Muzaffarpur — Shahi Litchi GI); makhana (Mithila — Darbhanga/Madhubani; Mithila Makhana GI); mango (Bhagalpur's Jardalu GI, Malda of the Diara). Green Revolution (1966–67): HYV seeds + fertiliser + irrigation; led by M.S. Swaminathan; transformed Punjab, Haryana and western U.P. — not eastern India, which is why Bihar's yields lag and the "second/evergreen revolution" debate centres on the east.

    Agro-climatic zones of Bihar — districts and signature crops

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    6.5 Minerals & Industry

    Exam-critical Bihar fact: the 2000 bifurcation transferred almost all mineral wealth (coal, iron ore, copper, uranium, mica belts) to Jharkhand. Bihar today has limited minerals: limestone (Rohtas/Kaimur — feeds cement plants), pyrite (Amjhore, Rohtas — for fertiliser/sulphuric acid), quartzite, bauxite (small, Munger), mica (Gaya–Nawada fringe of the old Koderma belt). BPSC's favourite trap: asking which mineral Bihar is rich in — the answer is essentially "none major, post-2000".

    All-India mineral map (memorise state associations): Coal — Gondwana fields: Jharia (Jharkhand — largest), Raniganj (W.B.), Talcher (Odisha); Iron ore — Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka (Bailadila, Kudremukh); Bauxite — Odisha (Panchpatmali); Mica — Jharkhand/Bihar (Koderma), Andhra; Copper — Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (M.P.); Petroleum — Mumbai High, Digboi (Assam — oldest refinery), Krishna-Godavari basin. Bihar industry: Barauni oil refinery (Indian Oil), Barauni fertiliser plant, sugar mills of north Bihar (many sick/revived), Bhagalpur silk handlooms.

    Quick revision hooks: Ganga 2,525 km · Son joins near Patna (south bank) · Kosi = "Sorrow of Bihar" · Falgu flows underground at Gaya · Kanwar Lake = Bihar Ramsar · Black soil = cotton · Kharif = rice, Rabi = wheat · 2000 bifurcation took Bihar's minerals to Jharkhand.

    7. Indian Polity & the Constitution

    Fundamental Rights — six groups (Art 12–35)

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    Panchayati Raj — three tiers (73rd Amendment)

    Redraw this from memory — every label is a potential one-mark answer.

    7.1 Framing the Constitution

    The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946); its first meeting was on 9 December 1946 with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha (from Bihar) as interim president. On 11 December 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad — also from Bihar — was elected permanent president. The Drafting Committee (29 August 1947) was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950 (chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj declaration of 26 January 1930). It is the world's longest written constitution — originally 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.

    Exam trap: 26 November is observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas); the Preamble, citizenship, elections and provisional parliament provisions took effect immediately on 26 Nov 1949, the rest on 26 Jan 1950.

    7.2 The Preamble

    "We the People of India…" — source of authority is the people. Key terms: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; Justice (social, economic, political); Liberty; Equality; Fraternity. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Socialist, Secular and Integrity. In Berubari (1960) the Preamble was held not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) reversed this — it is part of the Constitution and part of the basic structure, though not directly enforceable.

    7.3 Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35)

    RightArticlesNotes
    Right to Equality14–1814: equality before law; 15–16: non-discrimination; 17: abolition of untouchability; 18: abolition of titles
    Right to Freedom19–2219: six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession — property removed by 44th Amendment, 1978); 20–22: protection in conviction, life & personal liberty (Art. 21 — expanded by Maneka Gandhi, 1978 to include due process and dignified life), arrest safeguards
    Against Exploitation23–24Prohibition of begar/trafficking; child labour under 14 in hazardous work
    Religion25–28Freedom of conscience, practice, propagation
    Cultural & Educational29–30Minority language/script protection; minority-run institutions
    Constitutional Remedies32"Heart and soul" (Ambedkar); direct access to the Supreme Court

    Writs (Art. 32/226): Habeas Corpus (produce the body), Mandamus (command a public duty), Prohibition (stop a lower court), Certiorari (quash a lower court's order), Quo Warranto (by what authority do you hold office). Exam trap: Art. 32 can itself be suspended only during a National Emergency — and even then, per the 44th Amendment, Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended.

    7.4 Directive Principles & Fundamental Duties

    DPSP (Articles 36–51) — non-justiciable but "fundamental in governance" (Art. 37). Landmark ones: Art. 38 (welfare state), Art. 39A (free legal aid — 42nd), Art. 40 (Panchayati Raj), Art. 44 (Uniform Civil Code), Art. 45 (early childhood care — substituted by 86th), Art. 48A (environment — 42nd), Art. 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), Art. 51 (international peace). Minerva Mills (1980): balance between FRs and DPSP is part of the basic structure.

    Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) — added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; originally 10, now 11 after the 86th Amendment (2002) added the duty of parents/guardians to educate children aged 6–14.

    7.5 Union Government

    • President (Articles 52–62): elected by an electoral college (MPs + MLAs, not MLCs); 5-year term; impeachment (Art. 61) for violation of the Constitution; can promulgate ordinances (Art. 123) when Parliament is not in session; three veto types — absolute, suspensive, pocket (no pocket veto time limit is specified — the famous "pocket veto" usage). Trap: the President is not directly elected by the people.
    • Vice-President (Art. 63–71): ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; elected by MPs of both Houses.
    • Prime Minister & Council of Ministers (Art. 74–75): real executive; collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; the 91st Amendment (2003) caps ministers at 15% of the House strength.
    • Parliament: Lok Sabha (max 552; current strength 543 elected; 5-year term unless dissolved; Speaker presides) and Rajya Sabha (max 250; current 245; permanent body, 1/3 retire every 2 years; 12 nominated members). Money Bills (Art. 110): only in Lok Sabha, Speaker certifies, Rajya Sabha has 14 days; joint sitting (Art. 108) for deadlocks — used only thrice (Dowry Prohibition 1960, Banking Service Commission 1977, POTA 2002).

    How a Bill becomes an Act — the five-gate flowchart
